prompt: What is an equivalence partition?
hint: Where do the lines come from?

choices.text: A set of inputs the code happens to handle in one way
choices.why: The code is what is being tested; the partition comes from what it should do.

choices.text: A set of inputs the requirement says to treat alike
choices.why: Right: one value from it stands for the rest, and it can be drawn before any code exists.

choices.text: Every value the field accepts without showing an error
choices.why: That is one valid partition at most; the refused values form partitions too.

choices.text: A group of cases sharing a precondition
choices.why: Partitions divide inputs, not cases.

prompt: R2's table has eight partitions: three valid (name, password, e-mail) and five invalid. Following the lesson's rules, what is the smallest number of sign-up cases that covers all eight?
hint: Valid partitions can share a case; invalid ones cannot.

prompt: Which value is the best representative of the name partition "1 to 40 characters"?
hint: A representative speaks for the middle.

choices.text: A name of exactly 40 characters
choices.why: That is a boundary value; it gets a case of its own in the next technique.

choices.text: Five names of different lengths between 1 and 40
choices.why: Five values from one partition ask one question five times.

choices.text: A name of about 20 characters
choices.why: Right: from the middle, where it says how the whole partition behaves.

choices.text: A name of 41 characters, to see it refused
choices.why: That value belongs to another partition, the invalid one above.

prompt: A promotion field accepts any of 30 codes printed on a flyer and refuses everything else. Which partitions does it have?
hint: Not every partition is a range of numbers.

choices.text: A code on the flyer, and anything else
choices.why: Right: the rule treats the 30 alike and the rest alike, like R2's used and unused e-mail.

choices.text: One partition per code, thirty valid ones in all
choices.why: The rule does not treat any code differently from another, so they are one partition.

choices.text: Codes up to some length, and longer ones
choices.why: Nothing in the rule mentions a length; that partition is invented.

choices.text: Only the valid one, since every wrong code is refused the same way
choices.why: Refused input is a partition too, and it needs a case.

prompt: When can one representative from the middle of a partition miss a defect?
hint: The technique rests on an assumption.

choices.text: When the partition is a valid one rather than invalid
choices.why: Valid and invalid partitions rest on the same assumption.

choices.text: When the code splits it where the requirement does not
choices.why: Right: then the partition was not one, and the representative speaks for only part of it.

choices.text: When the requirement writes its range in numbers
choices.why: Numbers are what make a partition easy to draw.

choices.text: When the tester cannot read the code
choices.why: Partitions are drawn from the requirement, code or no code.

prompt: Why does boundary value analysis go to the edges of partitions?
hint: Think of one character of code.

choices.text: Edge values are the ones customers type most often
choices.why: Customers type middling values far more; edges are where code goes wrong.

choices.text: The middle of a partition is already covered by the code review
choices.why: Nothing in this lesson relies on a review.

choices.text: Extreme values crash programs
choices.why: Some do; the reason here is narrower.

choices.text: One wrong "<" moves the edge, and only an edge value sees it
choices.why: Right: every middle value behaves on both versions of the code.

prompt: R2 asks for a password of 8 to 64 characters. Which lengths does two-value boundary analysis test? Choose every one.
hint: Two lines, two values at each.

choices.why: The nearest invalid value below the lower line.
The smallest valid length, on the lower line.
One inside the line: three-value analysis adds it, two-value does not.
One inside the upper line, a three-value addition.
The largest valid length, on the upper line.
The nearest invalid value above the upper line.

prompt: A voucher works on orders up to R$ 100,00, that amount included. Which pair is two-value boundary analysis at that line?
hint: What is one step for money?

choices.why: A real is a hundred steps; a defect at R$ 100,50 would slip between them.
Right: the value on the line and the nearest one across it, one cent away.
Both are inside the valid partition; nothing tests the side where the voucher stops working.
Two representatives far from the line, and the line itself without its neighbour.

prompt: All eight of R2's boundary cases passed. What did running them produce?
hint: Before they ran, what did anybody know?

choices.text: Evidence that boxoffice draws R2's four lines where R2 draws them
choices.why: Right: a passing boundary case is a result, recorded like a failure.

choices.text: Nothing, since a boundary case earns its place by failing
choices.why: Before they ran, nobody knew where the lines were; now there is evidence.

choices.text: Proof that sign-up has no defects
choices.why: Eight cases say something about eight values and four lines, not about everything.

choices.text: A reason to drop R2's partition cases
choices.why: Boundary analysis is drawn on top of the partitions; it does not replace them.

prompt: At the name's upper line, two-value analysis tests 40 and 41, and three-value analysis adds ___ as well.
hint: The nearest value on the inside.

prompt: Which of the five quantity cases found the first defect?
hint: Six tickets.

choices.text: Q3, the 3 from the middle
choices.why: 3 was booked, as order 1002.

choices.text: Q5, the 7, one step above the valid range of R4
choices.why: 7 was refused, which is what R4 asks for.

choices.text: Q4, 6, the upper edge of the valid range
choices.why: Right: R4 allows six and boxoffice refused it.

choices.text: Q1, the 0, one step below the valid range of R4
choices.why: 0 was refused with a sentence, as R4 and R7 ask.

prompt: Six tickets was refused. Why did the lesson book five before writing anything down?
hint: Where is the line really?

choices.text: To check that the server was still up after the refusal
choices.why: The refusal came back as a page; the server was plainly up.

choices.text: To place the line: five booked puts it between 5 and 6
choices.why: Right: the result now says exactly where the edge is, off by one.

choices.text: To set up an order for the discount table in lesson 5
choices.why: Lesson 5 restarts boxoffice and books its own orders.

choices.text: Because a case is repeated before a failure counts
choices.why: Nothing here is flaky; the next value answers a different question.

prompt: Put the steps for a boundary case in the order the lesson takes them, from first to last.
hint: Expected comes before anything runs.
items: Write the expected result from R4
Compare what came back with the expected result
Try the neighbouring value to place the line
Record requirement, steps, expected, actual and what narrowed it
trap: Running the neighbour before comparing would narrow a failure nobody has seen yet.

prompt: A tester ran -3, 3 and 10 in the quantity field of boxoffice 1.0, and all three behaved. What did they miss, and why?
hint: Where do -3, 3 and 10 sit?

choices.text: Nothing: one value per partition covers the field
choices.why: It covers the partitions, and the defect is not in any of their middles.

choices.text: The traceback, as -3 is not a whole number
choices.why: -3 is a whole number, and it got its sentence; the traceback needs a non-number.

choices.text: Six being refused: none of the three sits on a line
choices.why: Right: partitions alone said R4 works; only an edge value shows the line is off by one.

choices.text: The 5-or-more discount, which is this field's
choices.why: The discount is R5, and it needs combinations, not single values.

prompt: A quantity of `two` answers 500 and a traceback. Which requirement does that break most directly?
hint: One requirement names error pages.

choices.text: R4, the rule of 1 to 6 tickets per order
choices.why: R4 says how many tickets are allowed, not how wrong input is answered.

choices.text: R7, a sentence and never an error page
choices.why: Right: it is an error page, and it says nothing a customer can act on.

choices.text: R9, use by keyboard and by screen reader
choices.why: Accessibility is about using the pages, not about this answer.

choices.text: R5, the prices, the discounts and how they combine
choices.why: No price was computed: the request failed before that.

prompt: `two` sent with an e-mail no account has answers "Sign up before you book." and no traceback. Why?
hint: Order matters inside the program.

choices.text: boxoffice checks the account first and stops there
choices.why: Right: the quantity is never read, so one invalid value masks the other.

choices.text: The traceback is shown to members, and the address is not one
choices.why: Who sees a traceback has nothing to do with membership.

choices.text: Two invalid values cancel each other out in the request
choices.why: Nothing cancels; the second value simply goes unread.

choices.text: The defect appears only for Hamlet
choices.why: The show was Hamlet in both requests.

prompt: Empty input, `2.5` and `two` each answer 500 in the quantity field. How should the result be written?
hint: Think of the partition.

choices.text: Three results, since each value is a separate case and a separate fault
choices.why: They are three cases, and the partitions say they show one fault.

choices.text: Only the `two` result, as the others are unlikely inputs
choices.why: Empty input is one of the likeliest; it is a slip of the thumb.

choices.text: One, naming the partition: anything that is not a whole number
choices.why: Right: stated as the partition, with the three values as evidence.

choices.text: No result, as the browser is meant to stop such input
choices.why: The browser does not stop it; the box accepts anything.

prompt: Match each quantity to the partition it belongs to.
hint: Is it a whole number, and if so, where does it fall?

prompt: Seven tickets came back with status 200 and a sentence; `two` came back with 500. What does the difference say?
hint: Who decided what?

choices.text: The second request reached another server, not boxoffice itself
choices.why: Both went to 127.0.0.1:8000.

choices.text: The 500 is simply the more polite of the two refusals
choices.why: A 500 is not a refusal at all, and it carried no sentence.

choices.text: A refusal boxoffice chose, against a failure it never handled
choices.why: Right: 7 met a check written for it, `two` met none.

choices.text: 7 is a valid quantity and `two` is not
choices.why: 7 is invalid too: R4 stops at 6.

prompt: A cinema gives a senior discount from age 60. Which two ages are two-value boundary analysis for that rule?
hint: The line sits between two ages.

choices.text: 60 and 61
choices.why: Both get the discount; nothing tests the side without it.

choices.text: 59 and 60
choices.why: Right: the last age without the discount and the first with it.

choices.text: 30 and 75
choices.why: Those are representatives of the two partitions, far from the line.

choices.text: 59 and 61
choices.why: They skip the value on the line itself, where "from 60" is decided.

prompt: Which of these quantities belong to an invalid partition of R4? Choose every one.
hint: Valid is 1 to 6, whole.

choices.why: In "0 or fewer".
The lower edge of the valid partition.
The upper edge of the valid partition, refused by boxoffice 1.0 by mistake.
In "7 or more".

choices.text: three
choices.why: Not a whole number written in digits.
A decimal is in the "not a whole number" partition, however round it looks.

prompt: When one invalid input stops a program before it reads a second, the second is hidden. This effect is called ___.
hint: A word for covering something up.
